processing: Medium oxidation with standard Wuyi shaking, strip-rolled and charcoal roasted to a medium level; a cultivar that does not need a heavy roast to show its fruit.
harvest_season: One spring picking, late April to early May, as mature shoots with three or four open leaves.
appearance_dry: Slender, tight, dark brown strips with a sweet, lightly smoky smell.
appearance_wet: Thick olive leaves with red rims, slightly narrower than Shui Xian, opening evenly.
taste_profile: Honeyed fruit (dried lychee, ripe peach) and a soft floral note over a medium body, with a gentle smoky-roasted edge and a cooling mineral finish.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, porcelain gaiwan. Short early steeps; the fruit is clearest in the second and third infusions and the mineral finish grows from the fourth.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year, roasted in early summer and sold from autumn with the year stated. With its medium roast it drinks well from release and for two to three years sealed and dry; it is rarely aged on purpose.
description:
Ban Tian Yao is the fifth name in the Wuyi famous-bush canon: when Da Hong Pao is set apart as the king, the list of four becomes Tie Luo Han, Bai Ji Guan, Shui Jin Gui and this one. It is a rock tea with more fruit and less roast than its companions, which makes it an easy way into the group.

The name is said three ways in Chinese, all pronounced ban tian yao: half-sky waist, half-sky hawk and half-sky demon. The common thread is the story of a bush found on a ledge halfway up the cliff of Sanhua Peak in the core scenic area; the hawk version has an abbot dreaming of a white hawk and a young monk climbing up to find a sprouting seed there. Treat all of that as folklore. The cultivar itself is real and is now propagated by cuttings and grown in modest quantities around Wuyi.

It is made like any yancha, picked mature in spring, shaken through the night to oxidise the leaf edges, then rolled and charcoal roasted. Makers usually keep the roast at a medium level, and the cup shows why: ripe peach, dried lychee and a honeyed sweetness come through clearly, with a faint smoky note from the roast and a mineral, slightly cooling aftertaste.

Brew it hot with a full gaiwan and quick pours. The second and third steeps are the most aromatic; by the fifth the fruit has faded into a smooth, sweet, mineral body that lasts several more infusions. It is not as thick as a good Shui Xian, and a heavy hand with steep times does not make it so.

Ban Tian Yao is scarce and mostly sold in small quantities by Wuyi specialists and as part of famous-bush tasting sets. Buy the current year's spring tea from a seller who states harvest and roast, and keep it sealed. If you like the fruity side of it, Shui Jin Gui is its closest relative in character.
sources_note: The Sanhua Peak cliff story and the three spellings are the standard Wuyi account, given here as folklore.
history:
Ban Tian Yao is a scarce Wuyi rock tea, counted among the five famous bushes in lists that add it to Da Hong Pao, Tie Luo Han, Bai Ji Guan and Shui Jin Gui. Its name is written several ways, 半天腰, 半天鹞, 半天妖 and 半天夭, which sound alike. The bush is placed on a cliff of Sanhua Peak near Jiulongke, and one account says the third of its peaks.

The usual story says the abbot of Tianxin Yongle temple dreamed of a white hawk coming down halfway up the peak, in one telling during the Ming Yongle reign, and sent a young monk who found a sprouting tea seed on the rock face. So it was named half-sky hawk, and the sound drifted to half-sky waist. That is legend. A firmer date is lacking too: one article says only that by tradition the bush existed by the late Qing.
